notes.title: You played, we collected your feedback! What are the results?
notes.content:
Hello, Mythbusters!

The playtests ended some time ago and we’ve been collecting your feedback! Thank you so much for your participation and engagement – all your remarks and suggestions are extremely valuable to us. So, what are the results?

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/35024330/d6b69f9130a3a8268b7f89be0ea76d82715f02f9.png[/img]

[b]A lot of you took part in the playtest, we were astounded![/b] The overall score is 4 out of 5 stars, or 80%, or 8/10 if you prefer these scoring systems. Most of you rated the gameplay, graphics and music 4/5, and the performance and atmosphere 5/5. That’s great results!

[list]
[*][b]What you seem to have liked most[/b] are the blueprint minigames, exploring the mechanics and tools at your disposal, the detailed interior of the workshop, and so on. 
[*]You liked the fact that you are involved in the myth from beginning to end, starting with the concept, creating all the necessary parts and ending with testing the myth out and creating an episode. 
[*]You were also thrilled with the customization elements, where you could use the parts you chose for the construction of tools and elements.
[/list]

[b]What did you think could be improved?[/b] You had some suggestions regarding for example the tutorial and camera control, and we’ve jotted down all of them. They were all valid notes!

All in all, you really enjoyed [b]the spirit of MythBusters[/b] in our game. You liked the atmosphere inside the workshop and being creatively engaged in all stages of the myth testing. You noted the realism of items and tools, and the details in the shop. You’d like background music to be added and to limit the number of screws and nails you need to hammer in 😁

Thank you so much for your participation and your feedback, none of it would be possible without you! Wishlist the full game, if you haven’t already, and…

See ya later!

notes.title: This month in science
notes.content:
Hello, Mythbusters!

The world of science never sleeps. Science experiments and groundbreaking discoveries happen at any time, any day, and anywhere. Even now, cures are being developed and technologies improved. Let us recap some of the more interesting events which happened this month in science.

[b]In Australia, scientists want to bring the Tasmanian Tiger back from extinction[/b]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/35024330/8f09b649fc7458384279fa3144895125782b6c3b.jpg[/img]
[i]Image credit: public domain via EJ Keller/The Smithsonian Institution[/i]

The Tasmanian Tiger, a marsupial known as Thylacine, has been believed extinct since 1936 when Benjamin, the last confirmed member of the species, died in captivity at Hobart’s Beaumaris Zoo. There have been rumoured sightings over the years but none were confirmed.

Scientists, however, were not ready to give up on the Tasmanian Tiger and have sequenced the genome, which might help bring the animal back from extinction. Now, scientists will have to develop an embryo and plant it successfully in the womb of a surrogate mother. Keep your fingers crossed for Thylacine!

[b]The black hole closest to the solar system turns out to not be a black hole[/b]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/35024330/ae5dc098035b1b4622ecb01403dea94fba0b6d86.jpg[/img]
[i]Image credit: Artist’s impression of HR 6819, CC BY 4.0[/i]

Two years ago, astronomers announced they have discovered a black hole closest to our solar system. The black hole was supposed to be a part of a three-body system, called HR 6819, consisting of two stars and a black hole. Well, turns out the HR 6819 is just two stars, no black hole included. However, these stars are certainly not ordinary.

It looks like the astronomers discovered the system just after one of the stars had its outer layer stripped by the other. The effect of this “stellar vampirism” made it look like the system includes an invisible black hole. This actually makes this discovery much more exciting, as the phenomenon of one star being stripped out of its atmosphere is very difficult to catch.

[b]One beer a day shrinks your brain[/b]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/35024330/1b12a0ef3e98d4f9cce3c04ca15afdd4d8ba94db.jpg[/img]
[i]Image credit: Nik Frey, CC BY 2.5[/i]

Or even half a bear, really. Recent studies seemed to highlight a dramatic difference in brain volume of alcohol drinkers compared to abstinents, and researchers from the University of Pennsylvania sought to delve deeper into the matter. 

Turns out, just one or two alcohol units a day lower the drinker’s brain volume, and the decrease gets worse the more alcohol is consumed. This new study challenges the common belief that small amounts of alcohol every day are beneficial to one’s health. So if you want to keep your brain younger, perhaps refrain from that one beer every day. It will also help you avoid any possible cognitive impairments.

[b]Mice with implanted “drug factories” are cured of cancer within a week[/b]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/35024330/06267861ce89bc81afd394820f49e3628a6af8d2.jpg[/img]
[i]Image credit: elements.envato.com, Commercial License[/i]

New cancer treatment is emerging. At this stage, it is still tested on mice but considering the excellent results, scientists may start the human trials as early as in the fall. Researchers have come up with an implant containing engineered human cells programmed to secrete interleukin-2, a cytokine that activates white blood cells to fight cancer and other diseases.

This cytokine is already used for cancer treatment but as an IV injection which often causes some undesirable side effects. The implant, however, is planted directly in the lining of a diseased organ and produces daily doses of the cytokine which combats the adjacent tumour until it’s gone. At this moment in time, this method fully cured all mice with ovarian cancer and 7 of 8 animals with colorectal cancer.

We hope this dose of news satisfied your science cravings for some time! Remember, stay safe and stay curious. If you want to help us, wishlist the game!

See you later, Mythbusters!

notes.title: This week in science: Pluto’s atmosphere is disappearing
notes.content:
Hello, Mythbusters!

Science is galloping forward every day, and while we’re waiting for the full game, we can spare a minute to catch up on the latest news straight from the scientific field. So what has happened this week?

The astronomers noticed that [b]Pluto’s atmosphere started to disappear![/b] Pluto is a dwarf planet (some of us still don’t agree with the new classification but that’s a topic for another time) which lies in the Kuiper Belt, over 4.8 billion kilometres (3 billion miles) away from Earth. When the planet was passing in front of our sun back in 2018, the astronomers were able to observe the curious change in its atmosphere, which the recently described in a new study.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/35024330/5d5debabf0eff0fa04e6dde241e346fddf7bfffc.jpg[/img]

Pluto’s atmosphere is primarily made out of nitrogen, just like Earth’s, and exists as a result of the vapours from the planet’s icy surface. It seems that the changes in surface temperature can dramatically impact the atmosphere’s density. To put it simply, the closer Pluto is to the Sun, the hotter its surface is. The hotter the surface, the denser the atmosphere becomes when ice turns into gas. And then it goes in reverse.

Pluto has been moving farther away from the sun for the last 25 years now and it seems that its atmosphere is actually refreezing back onto its surface due to the dropping temperature. So why is the atmosphere disappearing now if Pluto is already going further from the star? It’s all thanks to a phenomenon known as thermal inertia. Basically, Pluto had residual heat from when it was closer to the sun. Think of sand on the beach. It gathers the heat until noon when the sun shines the most but continues to burn your bare feet for at least a few more hours. The same happened with Pluto – only now has it started to lose the accumulated heat from the planet’s surface. It results in the nitrogen from the atmosphere turning back into ice and “glueing itself” back to the ice on the surface.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/35024330/a412e0d9dc32e9d27d36dd63d538529e20f1507c.jpg[/img]

And how did we know that? There is a method astronomers use to guess the density and size of a celestial body by observing the changes in the light of a star when an object passes in front of it. Because we already have an excellent density profile of Pluto obtained in 2015 during the New Horizons mission, astronomers noticed a change in the density of Pluto’s atmosphere when it was passing in front of the sun a few years later.

Science is fascinating, isn’t it? Would you like to hear more science facts like this one? If you can’t wait to make your own experiments, [b]wishlist Mythbusters: the Game and tell your friends about it.[/b] 
Stay tuned!
